description_full:
Corpay, Inc. operates as a payments company that helps businesses and consumers to manage and pay their expenses.
It operates through Corporate Payments, Vehicle Payments, Lodging Payments, and Other segments. The company offers vehicle payment solutions for fuel, tolls and parking, vehicle compliance, auto insurance and road assistance, fleet maintenance, and long-haul transportation services, as well as prepaid food and transportation vouchers and cards. It also provides corporate payment solutions, such as cross-border payments, spend management solutions, AP modernization, virtual cards, and purchasing and T&E cards. Additionally, it offers lodging payments solutions for employees who travel overnight for work purposes; traveling crews and stranded passengers from airlines and cruise lines; workforce lodging solutions for business travel programs; airline logistics, crew management, insurance, and other payments solutions. Further, the company offers gifts and payroll cards. It serves business, merchant, consumer, and payment network customers. The company was formerly known as FLEETCOR Technologies, Inc. and changed its name to Corpay, Inc. in June 2002. Corpay, Inc. was founded in 1986 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

Each employee generates $110K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $9K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Corpay, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $29.6B market cap on $4.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 8% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 29 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.40× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.9×.

Shareholder yield of 2.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.9% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 44% operating margin runs 37pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.88x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 41% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $178.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 45% below its DCF fair value of $834, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $556 to $1,239 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 12.7 vs 17.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 24% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $492 on average, 6% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It converts 29% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.40x.
ROE of 28% is amplified by 6.8x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.3% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.2x net debt to EBITDA ($2.4B of cash against $10.0B of debt), with interest covered 4.9x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.74 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.98 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.7% over 3 years, 13.6% over 5 years and 10.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (4.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 40, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (42 sales, net $146.4M sold).
It returns 2.4% a year to shareholders (2.4% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 4.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 11,800 employees, each generates about $384K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 16.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $110K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.4M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
